Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would like the indulgence of hon. members for a few moments before we get into the routine business of the house. The matter about which I wish to speak is something which has previously given the house concern, but during the past few weeks it has manifested itself more particularly. Our Hansard records have had a rather staccato appearance caused by gratuitous interjections into hon. members' speeches by other hon. members.
This creates a very difficult situation. The interjections themselves are quite out of order. I think all hon. members recognize that, and they leave a great responsibility upon the Hansard reporters and Hansard editor to determine, in effect, what are the proceedings of the house. I think it is recognized that this is not a task which should be laid upon them, and the position of acting as censor of Hansard is not one which is sought or ought to be sought by the Speaker.
It will be recognized that within, shall we say, earshot of the Hansard reporters, hon. members on both sides of the house appear to interject a great deal in debates and, frankly, some speeches are just riddled with interjections which are not heard either by the member who has the floor or by the Chair.
They actually consist of a sort of secondary debate by an hon. member who has not got the floor, in addition to which it permits certain hon. members to enter into a debate in a way which is not fair to other hon. members who sit further away from the Hansard reporters' table.
In this regard, I think all hon. members have equal rights in the house, but those hon. members who find themselves at the far end of the chamber and those who are much closer to the chair, if they would want to be heard in the same way would have to shout. Then of course we would be reduced to completely chaotic conditions in the house.
I offer these comments only in the spirit of maintaining the decorum of the house and the proprieties of the proceedings of the house,
and I trust hon. members will govern themselves accordingly. I think it is also known that unfortunately some very good speeches are ofttimes torpedoed by deliberate and gratuitous interjections that are not heard either by the person who has the floor or by the Chair. We cannot say that Hansard reporters or editors must themselves delete these interjections. In conclusion I ask hon. members to govern themselves accordingly in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADIAN RESOLUTION
subsubtopic: RESPECTING RADIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on
November 9 the special political committee of the general assembly unanimously approved the text of a resolution on radiation put forward by Canada and co-sponsored by 41 other member states. The vote was 79 in favour, none against, with 11 abstentions. The 11 abstaining countries were the Soviet union and its allies.
The Canadian delegation played a leading role in the drafting and negotiation which led to the unanimous adoption of this resolution. The resolution is divided into two sections. In the first part it asked the scientific committee of the United Nations to continue its assessment of radiation risks as well as its review of ways of increasing man's knowledge of the effects of radiation. It also calls the attention of all member states to the scientific committee's finding that "the exposure of mankind to radiation from increasing numbers of artificial sources including the world wide contamination of the environment with short and long lived radio nuclides from weapons tests, calls for the closest attention", since the effects of radiation increases may not be fully manifested until long after exposure has taken place.
The second part of the resolution commends the world meteorological organization for the plan it has prepared for the world wide monitoring and reporting of the levels of atmospheric radioactivity, and invites the organization to put a plan into operation as soon as possible after its final formulation. On an initiative taken by Canada last year the general assembly recommended that such
1500	HOUSE OF
Canadian Radiation Resolution Approved a plan for monitoring and reporting should be formulated, and implemented if found feasible.
I am sure all hon. members will realize the importance of such measures taken by the United Nations and associated agencies to promote the closest possible scientific cooperation at the international level, with a view to expanding man's knowledge of the effects of atomic radiation on human health. The approval of this resolution without opposition in the special political committee represents a significant forward step toward the achievement of this goal.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADIAN RESOLUTION
subsubtopic: RESPECTING RADIATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house will appreciate the importance of the passing of this resolution unanimously at the United Nations for the purpose of monitoring and measuring the effect of radiation in the atmosphere. I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree with me when I say that even more important is agreement at the United Nations to put an end to those activities which bring about the necessity for such measurement.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADIAN RESOLUTION
subsubtopic: RESPECTING RADIATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just like to add a word in this regard. I think the progress which has been made is encouraging, particularly as the resolution we are speaking about was passed with complete unanimity, and points towards the ending of nuclear testing. Certainly we have been made more aware of the dangers of radiation. We mentioned at the time of the Cuban crisis that some good might come out of that near tragedy, and certainly I think this is one of the things that is helping to bring people to their senses in regard to the dangers which face us and the possibility of our own destruction in this world of civilized progress.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CANADIAN RESOLUTION
subsubtopic: RESPECTING RADIATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, nature already provides sufficient hazards to human health without our also having to combat the man-made hazards resulting from nuclear testing. I am sure all hon. members will consider the resolution which has been passed at the United Nations, providing for the measuring and monitoring of the effects of radiation, to be a forward step. I am sure all of us will feel that the important step is to reach the stage where nuclear testing can be discontinued by unanimous agreement and under international inspection and control.

subtopic: POULTRY GRADING METHODS
POULTRY GRADING METHODS
speechtext: Has the Department of Agriculture instituted new grading methods or grading standards for poultry, particularly turkeys and, if so, how do these new procedures differ from previous methods, and what is the purpose of the change?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: POULTRY GRADING METHODS
speechtext:
The department has not instituted new grading methods or grading standards for poultry. However, agreement has been established between the Canadian turkey federation representing producers, the Canadian produce council representing the processors and the poultry division of the Department of Agriculture that some modification should and could be made in the amount of fat required for heavy turkeys that are eligible to be graded as Canada grade A. Agreement has also been established in the extent of the reduction desirable.
No request was made or consideration given to reducing the present standards with respect to amount and placing of meat on the bird or any other factors relating to grading.
The trend in breeding for heavier turkeys has resulted in the development of factors that brought about the need, in the interests of the industry, to modify the fat requirement in the grading of heavy turkeys: (1) Undesirable male characteristics were developing in the birds as a result of the additional feeding time necessary to attain the present fat level required, (2) The longer feeding period is costly to the producer from the standpoint of feed conversion, and, (3) It was becoming increasingly difficult to satisfactorily finish sufficient birds in this weight for the Thanksgiving market.
In view of the present popular trend to reduce fat in the human diet, it was considered that a slight reduction of fat requirement on these heavy birds could be undertaken without reducing the acceptability of the bird from the standpoint of consumer.
Agreement among the groups referred to was also reached that this new interpretation relative to fat requirement should be introduced for the marketing of the 1963 crop of turkeys.

speechtext: Would the government undertake to give consideration to proposing, at the appropriate international level, a 20 year non-aggression pact between members of the NATO and Warsaw pact powers?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NON-AGGRESSION PACT, NATO AND WARSAW POWERS
speechtext:
Consideration has been given for a number of years to the idea of a nonaggression	pact	between	NATO	and	theWarsaw pact powers. It has come up in the context of discussions of European security and of disarmament, and a variety of proposals have been made by both the Soviet union and the western allies. Such a pact would be repetitive of obligations assumed under the U.N. charter, but this need not necessarily rule out its usefulness. A nonaggression	pact	between	NATO	and	the
Warsaw pact powers might prove a useful adjunct to a broader settlement of outstanding east-west issues, though in itself and in isolation it would not materially contribute to the world's security. We are, however, keeping the possibility under review in consultation with our NATO allies and in the framework of the current disarmament negotiations.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: TELECAST OF GREY CUP GAME
TELECAST OF GREY CUP GAME
speechtext:
1.	Did the C.B.C. indicate to the B.B.G. that they were prepared to carry the telecast of the Grey cup game at any point during the negotiations between the B.B.G., C.T.V., C.B.C., and any other interested and involved parties and, if so, what were the terms of the proposal of the C.B.C.?
2.	Did C.T.V. offer to the C.B.C. the right of carrying the telecast of the Grey cup game without carrying the advertising that will be associated with the C.T.V. telecast of the Grey cup game?
3.	On what grounds did the B.B.G. compel the C.B.C. to carry the telecast of the Grey cup game complete with associated advertising sold by C.T.V.?
4.	Did the C.B.C. make any proposals during the course of the negotiations dealing with the Grey cup game telecast as to how this matter might be resolved and, if so (a) what were these proposals (b) were these proposals considered by the B.B.G. and (c) why were these proposals not acceptable to the B.B.G.?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: TELECAST OF GREY CUP GAME
speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows:
1.	Yes. The C.B.C. on several occasions indicated to the B.B.G. that it was anxious to televise the Grey cup game on its national networks provided that this did not involve sponsorship arrangements for C.B.C. networks that were determined directly or indirectly by C.T.V. and the corporation made a number of different proposals to this effect.
2.	The C.B.C. did receive such an offer but this offer was subsequently withdrawn.
3.	(answered by B.B.G.)
4.	Yes. (a) Certain proposals were made by the C.B.C. prior to the public hearing of the B.B.G. held August 18, 1962. These were reviewed in some detail at the hearing and additional proposals were put forward at that time. All of these form part of the record of that hearing, (b) (To be answered by the B.B.G.) (c) (To be answered by the B.B.G.)
I am informed by the board of broadcast governors as follows:

1.	If the holder of the rights agrees the C.B.C. will instal its own cameras and equipment at the Grey cup stadium and make its own pickup of the game at no cost to C.T.V. in any way. It is prepared to do this on a commercial-free basis or with sponsors of its own choice and is further prepared to provide C.T.V. with a clean feed.
2.	The C.B.C. will accept and broadcast the C.T.V. pickup of the game on a sustaining or commercial-free basis. The C.B.C. would require that the C.T.V. provide a clean feed that is without commercial or promotional material.
3.	The C.B.C. will accept and broadcast a clear feed of the C.T.V. pickup of the game on a commercial-free basis but will provide for five insertions in the broadcast of customary courtesy announcements which will name the C.T.V. sponsors and extend the appreciation of the corporation to them for making the C.B.C. coverage possible. In addition, the C.B.C. was prepared to offer commercial participation to C.T.V. sponsors on the C.B.C. network in programs prior to and following the Grey cup broadcast.
I am informed that none of these proposals were acceptable to the owners of the television rights of the game.
The B.B.G. was informed that these proposals had been made directly to the C.T.V. Television Network Ltd.
Reasons for the action of the board on the Grey cup game, November 7, 1962:
1.	Since the purchase of football rights by parties other than the C.B.C. the situation has remained chaotic and efforts to find voluntary solutions have proved futile. Some imposed solution seemed unavoidable.
2.	The Broadcasting Act, section 10, reads: "The board shall . . . regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto". The problem of the broadcast of the 1962 Grey cup game was largely one of the networks and the relations between them. The board's responsibility seemed clear.
3.	The board determined:
(a)	The owners of the rights were prepared to buy the C.T.V. network alone. The board did not feel that this solution was in the public interest.
(b)	The owners of the rights were prepared to buy the C.B.C. network alone. This solution would have provided complete coverage. However, the C.B.C. remained adamant that they would not, under any conditions, carry the commercials of the sponsors within the broadcast of the game.
Questions
(c)	The C.B.C. was prepared to take a clean feed from C.T.V. network and carry the broadcast on a sustaining basis. Because this would split the audience in the major markets, it was not acceptable to the owners of the rights.
The board has no authority over the owners of rights; its authority extends only to broadcasters, and can be exercised only by regulation.
4.	The board considered carefully the reasons for the adamant refusal of the corporation to accept the commercials for British-American Oil, Nabob and Labatt's under any conditions.
The corporation is engaged in commercial operations and has been increasingly aggressive in its commercial policy. The corporation has recently, because of reduced public revenues, found it necessary to cut its costs and curtail its service. The corporation has carried the broadcast of the Grey cup game in other years on a commercial basis. The three companies-B.A., Nabob and Labatt's -have all been acceptable sponsors to the C.B.C. over the years. The C.B.C. was willing to take the commercials of the three companies in the pregame and postgame programs; but not within the body of the broadcast of the game.
Why does the corporation find it so essential to refuse the sponsorship of these three companies at this time?
The corporation has said publicly that this year C.T.V. network and the sponsors conspired to sell and to buy the network of the C.B.C. The board knows of no evidence to support this claim. The board understands that in its contract with the sponsors C.T.V. network undertook to endeavour to secure coverage of the C.B.C. network, but agreed that if it failed to succeed in this the rights to the Grey cup game would be turned over to the sponsors. The transfer took place on October 1, 1962. The sponsors, as owners of the rights, were prepared to buy C.B.C. network alone. This proposal was rejected by the C.B.C. The owners of the rights were prepared to buy the C.T.V. network alone. This action did not seem to the board to be in the public interest.
The corporation has said that their object is to "teach a lesson" to CFTO-TV, C.T.V. network, and the sponsors, and other potential purchasers of the rights to football games, including the Grey cup game, and so to discourage or prevent any repetition of the events of the past two years. The inescapable fact is that there is now a second television network which will continue to extend its coverage and to improve its relative capacity to provide service to the population of Canada. Competition for the rights to popular events is here, and the conditions of competition on

Questions
a commercial basis will become more nearly equal. C.T.Y. network, and its affiliated stations, will be in the market for popular events. No disciplinary action on the part of the C.B.C. will change the situation.
It has been the consistent position of the board that even if C.T.V. network does not yet have the same coverage as the publicly owned network, it should not for that reason be excluded from all the popular events which call for wide coverage. The board believes that C.T.V. network should find it possible to carry some football games, and to have some participation in the annual Grey cup game broadcast. What is needed is some orderly basis for division of these events between the two networks.
Early in October the president of the C.B.C. approached the president of C.T.V. network to discuss an agreement over a term of years which would incorporate the principle of dividing the distribution of football broadcasts. This responsible approach to the problem nearly succeeded. It failed, in part, because of unreconciled but negotiable differences on the conditions for the future; it failed, mainly, because the agreement would have provided for a solution of the 1962 problem, the C.B.C. carrying the commercials of B.A., Nabob and Labatt's The C.B.C. board of directors refused to accept this condition for a long run settlement.
It is obvious that further efforts must be made to establish a basis on which the two networks will be prepared to distribute football broadcasts-a basis which includes division of the broadcasts. The board earlier wrote to all the parties involved suggesting a meeting to discuss the permanent problem and to seek a permanent solution. In view of the move by the president of the C.B.C. and his direct approach to C.T.V. network, no further action was taken by the board. This approach having failed, the board will resume its efforts to get the parties together.

MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for leave, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming, to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a matter of definite, urgent public importance, namely the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture concerning the advisability of burdening western wheat growers with a portion of any loss which might be incurred through credit sales of wheat abroad and of placing upon wheat producers' organizations some of the responsibilities now borne by the Canadian wheat board.
If there is any question about the matter of urgency, I should like to raise the point that the Minister of Agriculture has asked the wheat growers of western Canada to consider these two propositions, and I submit that before constituents discuss them members of parliament should have the opportunity to discuss the implications of these two proposals, which in my opinion are simply a devious means of undermining the scope and function of the Canadian wheat board.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in connection with the application which has just been made, it is my understanding that it has always been the rule that urgency of debate is the criterion by which such matters must be determined. With respect to this instance, I would point out that we had a supply motion last Monday and Tuesday, at the end of which the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were introduced. Therefore I suggest that in due course the estimates of this department will come before the house, and there will then be an opportunity to debate the question which the hon. member has raised. I suggest that the urgency of debate is not sufficient at the present time to warrant the interruption of the regular proceedings of the house to discuss this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is a matter not only of urgency but of immediate urgency and of obvious importance in view of the actual text, which is in our hands, of the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture and the uneasiness that this speech, in some respects at least, must have aroused. Surely it is important to clarify the situation at once with regard to

Grain Losses on Credit Sales this matter, especially in respect of the following sentence of the minister's speech, when he said:
I wish to make it perfectly clear that I am not suggesting that farmers take the entire risk of a loss on a credit sale.
The hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said that this is not a matter of urgency, in that we had a supply motion last week. That is true, but we do not know when we are going to have another supply motion when we could bring up this matter. We do not know when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are going to be brought before the house. If we were given some assurance that these estimates would be before us in the next day or two, perhaps that would be the appropriate time; but in the absence of such assurance I suggest that this is a matter of importance, and of immediate and urgent importance, and justifies the motion that has been made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the views expressed by the Leader of the Opposition, I think what he says is perfectly reasonable and that an opportunity should be given to discuss this matter. On Wednesday it is our intention to call the agriculture estimates, so that every opportunity will be given to members of the house to discuss this matter.
However, in view of the reference made by the Leader of the Opposition to the text of the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, who is unfortunately absent on official business today, I would point out that on page 1 it is made perfectly clear that the expression of these views in no way represents government policy.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition has quoted from the remarks made and I wish to complete the quotation. The Minister of Agriculture said:
I want to put forward a series of proposals, which are in my mind, in the hope there will be public discussion during the winter on these matters.
I emphasize that there is no possibility of any of these matters being considered until the farmers have cogitated on them and discussed these questions for a period of months. Therefore on both grounds there is not that urgency, I suggest, which would permit the adjournment of the house.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whether or not the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture last week end were official government policy, certainly they have aroused a great deal of concern among the farmers of western Canada and a lot of other people as well. I am pleased to


hear the Prime Minister say that we are going to have an opportunity to discuss this matter in the immediate future. I trust that we can go ahead with this discussion.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka pointed out that there was a supply motion last week. The statements to which I refer were made only last Friday, and there has been no other opportunity to present this matter to the house.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to speak in reply but merely to clarify one point. When I raised the question of a supply motion I did so to show that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture had been introduced for discussion and that in due course the estimates themselves would be coming up for discussion in committee. The Prime Minister has now assured the house that that will be the case, and that they will come forward promptly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Order. It will be recognized that any motion under standing order 26 is a very extraordinary remedy, and that the matter raised must be of very grave and sudden importance. It is recognized that while there are a large number of important matters, we always go to the question of whether they are important enough that debate is so urgently required at the very moment that the house must set aside its ordinary business. That is the principle that underlies the use of standing order 26.
I would refer hon. members for verification in this regard to citation 100 in Beauchesne, which clearly indicates that there must be urgency of debate:
-when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.

In the light of the fact that the agriculture estimates have been called, that the Minister of Agriculture indicated that this matter was for consideration, that no particular plan was going into effect immediately and that he wished individuals to consider it; in view of the fact that it has been announced that the agriculture estimates will be called on Wednesday; and finally taking into consideration a further quotation from Beauchesne:
The adjournment of the house cannot be moved with reference to critical conditions generally prevailing in certain parts of the country.
I feel the claim by the hon. member moving this motion, that there is a great deal of consternation among farmers in western Canada, is not sufficient under this standing order.
For those reasons I consider this motion does not qualify under standing order 26 in so far as the urgency of immediate debate is concerned. Therefore the motion is not in order.

Resolved,-That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide among other things:
1.	That the present exemption from sales tax for "books, printed and bound, that contain no advertising and are solely for educational, technical, cultural or literary purposes," be changed to read "printed books that contain no advertising and are solely for educational, technical, cultural or literary purposes".
2.	That audio tapes and materials used in the manufacture thereof, authorized by the department of education of any province in Canada for instruction in the English and the French language, be exempt from sales tax.
3.	That baler twine and materials used in the manufacture thereof be exempt from sales tax, regardless of use.
4.	That barrels and boxes for fish, lobster crates, lobster pots, lobster traps, scallop bags, and materials used in the manufacture thereof be exempt from sales tax.
5.	That drums or cans for honey and materials used in the manufacture thereof be exempt from sales tax.
6.	That goods for use in sewerage and drainage systems and materials used in the manufacture thereof be exempt from sales tax.
7.	That the present liability for sales tax on motor vehicles, tractors and machines and tools operated by such vehicles or tractors, that are diverted from an exempt use to a taxable use, be limited to five years from the time of the first sale by a person who would have been required to pay sales tax if the sale had not been for an exempt use, and where motor vehicles, tractors and machines and tools operated by such vehicles or tractors were imported or sold by a manufacturer or licensed wholesaler and sales tax was not payable or was refunded by reason of the intended use of the goods, any person who within five years of such importation or sale applies the goods to any other use (other than of a casual nature) for which the goods could not originally have been purchased exempt from sales tax, and the person from whom he purchased or rented the goods including the importer, manufacturer or licensed wholesaler, shall be jointly and severally liable for payment of sales tax on the fair market value of the goods at the time they are applied to that other use.
8.	That the present tax of 10 per cent on net premiums in respect of insurance against risks in Canada paid or payable by Canadian residents to an insurer not authorized under the laws of Canada or any province to transact the business of insurance, be extended to apply to net premiums in respect of any such insurance paid or payable by or on behalf of Canadian residents, where such insurance is entered into or renewed through a broker or agent outside Canada with an insurer that at the time the contract is entered into or renewed is authorized under the laws of Canada or any province to transact the business of insurance.
9.	That any enactment founded on paragraphs 1 to 6 of this resolution be deemed to have come into force on April 11, 1962, that any enactment founded on paragraph 7 of this resolution shall come into force on the date the said enactment is assented to, and that any enactment founded on paragraph 8 of this resolution be applicable in respect of contracts of insurance entered into or renewed after April 10, 1962.

I refer to their request for the exemption of farmers' fencing from sales tax. I find also, as I have found for quite a few years, that those things that the present minister and the former minister once talked about as being worth while and deserving of sales tax exemption have not been taken care of. I recall that when the former minister of finance was on this side of the house in opposition in 1957, in his last speech in opposition with respect to financial

matters, he said that he thought it was outrageous that clothing, boots and shoes, and necessities of that kind bore this very substantial sales tax. We feel that even the new minister has had plenty of time to bring before this delayed session of parliament, after an election, something new and fresh by way of a budget, particularly having regard to the economic necessities of the country at the present time, and we think the matter of a second budget cannot be delayed if we are to keep this country in good health.

Mr. Chairman, having regard to the first part of the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, perhaps this would be the appropriate time for me to introduce the proposed amendment. Therefore I move, seconded by the Minister of Finance:
That paragraph 7 of the Excise Tax Act resolution be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
7. That where a motor vehicle or tractor, or a machine or tool for operation by a motor vehicle or tractor, has been purchased or imported by a person who is the first purchaser or importer of the article for his own use and the article was purchased or imported for a use rendering such puchase or importation exempt from sales tax, or where any such article has been purchased or imported by a user to whom the sale or by whom the importation was exempt from sales tax, if within five years of such sale or importation the article is
(a)	applied by the purchaser or importer to any use (other than of a casual nature) for which it could not originally have been purchased or imported exempt from sales tax, or
(b)	sold or leased by the purchaser or importer and such sale or lease is not exempt from sales tax, the said purchaser or importer shall be deemed to have sold the article at the time of the said application, sale or lease and sales tax shall be payable on its value at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should just like to make a brief explanation of this. I know it is in highly technical language. I must say I read it through myself several times, and I am not yet sure I can explain it satisfactorily. But I am satisfied of this, that the amendment meets the objection which my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River, I think quite properly, raised to this whole section. He will know, having sat on this side of the house in days when there was criticism of this, that the Department of
Excise Tax Act
National Revenue took the position that if goods were sold-tractors or whatever they may be-which were exempt from tax, and then afterwards they were found in the hands of a person other than the original purchaser, then the department could follow the machinery through and also to go back to the original vendor, the manufacturer or whoever it may be.
In an attempt to meet this criticism-and I personally must say, having been minister of national revenue, that I thought there was some merit in the criticism-my predecessor, the former minister of finance, had an amendment introduced in his budget last year which imposed a five year limit during which these steps could be taken. Following that objections were raised by manufacturers, agents, brokers and so on, who were handling these types of machines, similar to the criticism raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River a few minutes ago, namely that it was unfair to hold liable for tax the original purchaser, or the broker who had sold a machine bona fide for tax exempt purposes, for instance a tractor for lumbering operations, the broker having satisfied himself that the purchaser was going to use it for such lumbering purposes, which purposes were tax exempt. That being the case, the purchaser or the original agent should not be held responsible for the fact that somebody sold it for a taxable purpose within five years.
Therefore the section is being amended so that if a machine is bought for a tax exempt purpose, and the original vendor or manufacturer has satisfied himself as to the purpose, he could not then be held responsible for the tax because later on the machine had got into the hands of somebody who purchased it for a taxable purpose. In other words, a man buying a tractor for lumbering operations could sell it to a farmer and it would still be tax exempt; but if it was sold to a contractor, shall we say, for the purpose of road building or something of that kind, then the tax could be collected from the person who bought it. But you cannot go back to the original vendor who had made the sale honestly, after advice and investigation, and believing he had made a bona fide sale to a bona fide purchaser for a tax free purpose. Tax could not be collected from that person. I think that despite the rather lengthy, involved and technical language, this amendment boils down to the very complaint which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River raised.

As I have said earlier, Mr. Chairman, after these resolutions are passed, if the committee sees fit to pass them, we will bring forward the bills dealing with income tax, excise tax, estate tax and the customs tariff. We will be prepared then to deal with them at any time after tomorrow that the committee wishes to deal with them, but they are not to be dealt with tomorrow in accordance with the arrangements that have been made.
There are only ten tariff amendments in these resolutions, and I might say that is the smallest number in any tariff resolutions for a great many years. They are all of a

relieving nature. Five of them provide for the extension without change of statutory provisions which have terminal dates of July 1, 1962. In other words, there are some provisions here which would have expired on July 1, 1962 were it not for the budget that was introduced in April. These are postponed in one case for one year and in other cases for two years.
The other items involve the removal of duties either through the establishment of a new free item or by expanding the scope of existing free items. For instance, there is something about blood plasma there and some element entering into it, the name of which I frankly could not pronounce if the committee asked me to do so. This has now been placed on the free list. There are several items of that nature but altogether we are dealing with a resolution with ten items, five of which extend the time and the other five of which are relieving in nature. There is nothing which increases the incidence of the tariff burden in any way.

Mr. Chairman, I expect to be brief at this stage. As the minister says, the actual number of items is unusually small but I must take issue both with the language that the new minister has used today and that used by his predecessor when he introduced the budget and said that all the amendments would be in a downward direction. That might have been true last April. However, just as was the case when we were discussing the matter of lobsters under the Excise Tax Act a short time ago, it is quite possible in my opinion that while it was true then that all these changes would have been of a relieving nature and the duties would have gone down if the changes had been made by parliament, the fact is that I believe that these items before us in the schedule are not free throughout the three categories and will bear some duty under the general tariff. The general tariff was normally meaningless but as a result of the action taken by order in council last June to impose surcharges these items will bear duty from that date and in some cases a substantial cost of duty.
I am thinking of items such as aircraft or aircraft engines which I would imagine we would never import under the general tariff under any circumstances but rather always import under the British preferential tariff or the most favoured nation tariff, both of which provide free entry. As a result of the surcharge order in council, which we claim is illegal if not ratified by parliament, these aircraft items will bear duty from now on of at least 5 per cent. I have not checked to see whether they are in the 5

per cent surcharge category or 10 per cent or 15 per cent. I want to point out that as a result of the so-called austerity surcharges anyone importing an aircraft or an aircraft engine, which is a very costly thing, of a type not made in Canada will have to pay a rate of duty of 5 per cent at least.
When we come to the discussion on second reading of the bill I hope the minister will give us more information than he did in answer to my question the other day. As found on page 1275 of Hansard for November 5, I asked about the negotiations with reference to the surcharges and GATT. In essence he simply told me that all we were entitled to know was that negotiations were proceeding. Having regard to the world trade situation and the world interest in tariffs, I hope that the minister will have more to say with respect to the relationship of these surcharges and the general amendment of the Customs Tariff Act, because as far as I can see the general agreement on tariffs and trade contains no provision which contemplates import surcharges such as Canada has established.
While we on this side do not propose to hold up the minister this afternoon on the details of these amendments, I want to indicate to him that we feel that on second reading of the bill it would be appropriate for him to give us a little more information than what I would term the brush-off answer he gave in reply to my question the other day as well as in reply to the hon. member for Rosedale, I believe, who asked a similar oral question last week.
There is one other matter I should like to put before the minister and perhaps his parliamentary secretary would help me with regard to it before we come to the debate on the bill. I wonder what the procedure is vis-a-vis the surcharge order in council with respect to an item in the schedule that was not in the tariff schedule before the budget of last April. I am thinking of item 220b. In looking over the order in council of June 25, I find no reference to item 220b although it is an item that does call for a general rate of duty. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary will advise me on the procedure in that regard. I am simply wondering how it was dealt with. Does it escape the minimum 5 per cent surcharge simply because it was an item introduced for the first time in the budget of last April or is it an oversight in the four days panic of surcharge schedules, about which we have been told?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house but, speaking for a certain number of people in the country, there are a few points I should like to bring before the house for consideration. First I should like to refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) when we were considering the bill previously. All members of the house recognize and appreciate the interest of the hon. member in the thalidomide tragedy. Nevertheless, I do not think it would be fair to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) if we let the remarks of the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) pass without referring to them. I would like to quote just briefly from the speech of the hon. member for York Centre on these particular amendments, when he said:
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) felt it was necessary to take what I feel is a retrograde step in this whole tragedy and go back to the place where we were last July, when public utterances were made by some people who were not personally acquainted with this tragedy, and attempt to find out who was to blame and leave it at that.
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking to this bill he was speaking as an individual who is highly concerned with this particular tragedy and highly concerned with and interested in the health, welfare and safety of the Canadian people. What he said is backed up, supported and appreciated by all members of this particular group. As the hon. member for York Centre indicated when he was addressing the house, surely nobody in Canada is interested in attempting to make political hay out of the thalidomide tragedy. What we are interested in is looking to the future. We agree it is not appropriate that we should concentrate on the past exclusively.
Therefore, we criticize the government, yes, for some of the things that were done and not done; but we do so, we hope, constructively. We seek not to blame any particular individual or any group, but rather to impress upon the government and the departmental personnel concerned the need for change and the need for safeguards for the safety of the public. Thalidomide, as it happens, is in the spotlight and has been for some

time; but the scope of the whole drug industry is really involved in these particular amendments, because surely when we are talking about the Food and Drugs Act we are concerned with the whole spectrum of the drug industry in Canada and its operations as they bear on the health, welfare and safety of the people.
We pay tribute, of course, with all others to the wonders of science in this age and to the dedicated scientists and other personnel in our food and drugs directorate. But at the same time it is not sufficient to be sorry for tragedies that have taken place. We must be resolved that we are going to protect the consuming public, those people who are using drugs and those people who must use various drugs. We must protect them against the over-anxious drug profiteers; and we have some of them. There are some people engaged in the drug industry who are not particularly concerned with the health of the individuals consuming these drugs; they are interested only in the profits they can make as a result of engaging in this particular industry. Certainly we agree with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) that we do not want to place restrictions in the way of the industry so as to impede valuable research and hold up the discovery of new drugs. Certainly we want, with all others, to defend the right of the industry to seek reasonable profits as they cautiously pursue the objectives of their industry. But regardless of our interests in not impeding research and in protecting the rights of the industry, surely it is of just as much importance, if not of more importance, that we look to the safety of the public. It is with this particular aspect that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-and, I am quite sure, many other hon. members of this house-is concerned.
During the course of the debate the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Mar-coux) made some contradictory statements with regard to the role of the government in the food and drugs industry. For his information and for the information of some people who may not be so sure that the government has a proper role to play in this field, I would like to refer to the timing involved in the thalidomide tragedy, pointing out the extremely useful role played by the food and drug administration in the United States. I think this becomes very evident when we recognize that thalidomide was first introduced to Canada in April of 1961. I repeat, April of 1961. It was removed from the market on March 2, 1962. But in the United States a government agency-granted, as a result of the efforts and the vigilance of
Food and Drugs Act
Dr. Kelsey-discovered that there was the possibility of some undesirable features, some threat to safety, in February of 1961. This was a result of research which had been conducted in the United States beginning back in 1959. Therefore in the United States it was discovered that there was a degree of unsafeness with regard to thalidomide in February of 1961. Nevertheless, two months later, in April of 1961, this same drug was placed on the market here in Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, we return to the main points of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he was speaking on these amendments some days ago. One of the steps we must be concerned with is staffing our department so that in future they will have a sufficient number of personnel and enough desirable equipment to prevent this type of tragedy occurring. We need more people; it is as simple as that; and we need more and better facilities. It is an established fact that unsafe drugs can reach the market. It can be established that their immediate withdrawal at some point in the future would be desirable. Swift and decisive removal would be the order of the day. Therefore it seems to us that the federal government department concerned should give some consideration to introducing legislation which will give them this right and which will give them the power to quickly, and without any question, have a drug removed from the market at the penalty of the manufacturer and the retailers concerned. But more important again, steps must be taken by the government to make sure that the drug does not reach the market in the first place.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am going to try to be brief. One of my colleagues will have a little more to say a little later on about this legislation. We are looking forward to the report later on this session of the restrictive trade practices commission into the whole question of drug prices in Canada. But for the moment I would like to suggest to the minister that it is about time that we in Canada started placing some responsibility on the drug manufacturers in this country to prove, not only the safety of their compounds, but also the value of the particular article which they are purporting to present to the public with some advantageous result on their health. They should be required, also, to discover and indicate to physicians, pharmacists and patients undesirable side effects in their drugs. We would suggest that a complete analysis, for example, should be sent along with samples when they are forwarded to practising physicians. We would suggest that consideration should further be given so that advertisements of drugs, whether on

Food and Drugs Act
radio, television or in the press, should summarize the dangerous side effects in relation to any particular other condition that may exist in that particular patient.
We are also concerned that in presenting drugs to the public they should be provided with the generic name of the drug as well as the trade or brand name, in order that they might really have the opportunity to buy their products in a competitive market place. In short, it is quite evident that within the scope of the whole drug industry in Canada our safety standards are somewhat dubious and the present levels of profits in this industry are certainly questionable, if not excessive.
In concluding, I say once again that the main points we are asking the government to consider are those put forward by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-the need for a stronger food and drug department, the need for additional staff to work in this field, and the need for greater protection for the public who are using these drugs daily.

subtopic: FOOD AND DRUGS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
The
purpose of this bill is to protect the health of the Canadian people. That is a laudable object, but it is unfortunate that in bringing forth this measure the government should have restricted itself to a most narrow construction of the problems which confront it.
It is unfortunate that, faced by the dangers which have now become apparent as a result of the use of the drug thalidomide, the government should merely be proposing a holding operation. It is proposing a couple of amendments intended to plug a few of the more obvious leaks in the legislation we now have. It is a pity, in my opinion, that the government did not take this opportunity to enact bolder legislation based on a detailed study of the extensive investigation which was made by the Kefauver committee in the United States Senate and also by the director of research of the combines investigations branch of the Department of Justice here in Canada. Had this been done, the bill we are considering at the present time would have been vastly different from the one which is now before us.
It is not enough to say that the measures which are now being proposed are worth while. We should be considering further steps which would be of equal or greater importance to the Canadian people.
It is, of course, impossible to be completely certain that all dangers have been eliminated when a new drug is put on to the market. If we waited long enough for that, there would probably never be new drugs on the market. But the Canadian people have a right to expect that all reasonable precautions have

been taken and that adequate clinical tests have been made by responsible, objective and conscientious authorities. I wish to make it clear I have no criticism to direct against the people in the department-the people who work for the federal government. I must say I found the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) completely incomprehensible, because without the protection given by the government departments both here and in the United States we would be left completely at the mercy of the private drug companies, and there is ample evidence that these are more interested in making profits than they are in the health and welfare of the people they supposedly serve.
If we are to have the kind of careful research which is needed, one thing is obvious, from the report of the Kefauver committee and, indeed, from the report submitted to the Department of Justice: the practice we have followed in the past of depending to an overwhelming extent upon the research facilities of the private drug companies is simply not good enough. For one thing, the research facilities of the Canadian drug companies are lamentably limited. One could spend days, or weeks, going over the records, particularly with regard to the research and marketing methods used by drug companies in the United States. I refer to them because to a large extent the Canadian drug companies are controlled and dominated by their parent United States organizations.
Dr. Kempe, professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Medical School says that "advertising claims made for each antibacterial agent are always unduly enthusiastic and sometimes misleading. In many cases," he said, "these multiple drugs reflect the competitive nature of the drug business rather than therapeutic need." Advertising pressure on doctors by the drug companies has been fantastic^ Charles Pfizer, one of the largest drug companies in the United States, circulated doctors in 1958 about a new broad spectrum antibiotic stating that it was highly effective and clinically proved. The advertisement sent to doctors gave names and addresses of doctors who had apparently used the new preparation. Upon investigation by the editor of a reputable scientific magazine, these names and addresses were found to be fictitious. Drug companies have been loath to police the industry, and the doctors themselves are too busy to check all the claims which are made for new drugs by the drug companies.
Where else but to the government may we turn to give protection to the doctors who will have to prescribe these drugs or to the

patients who will use them? It is obvious that the staff we presently have, competent though it may be, finds itself unable to do more than the very minimum of spot checking of the thousands of new drugs which appear on the market every year. Dr. William Bennet Bean of the Iowa State University School of Medicine and chairman of the board of regents of the national library of medicine said in testimony before the Kefauver committee:
The scientific and medical people (in drug companies) who make and test drugs find themselves at odds with the marketing, advertising and sales divisions but without a strong voice in controlling events. The business promotes the interests of the stockholders . .. the stockholder's appropriate interest is in income. The richest earnings occur when a new variety is marketed before competing drugs can be discovered, improved, named and released. This bonanza time may last only a few months. Unless there are large earnings, the quick kill with the quick pill, the investment does not pay off. Commercial secrets must be kept dark, lest a competitor get the jump.
Long tests as to use and potential dangers are not practical, since they have to be done in hospitals and medical schools where secrecy cannot be tolerated. While we ourselves have such a small staff it is idle to expect the Canadian people to be protected against drug companies which are interested in getting their products on the market as effectively as possible. There is only one agency which can provide this protection for the Canadian people and it is the appropriate department of the federal government in co-operation with the various medical schools and other scientific departments of the universities. In introducing the bill the minister made no suggestion that we could expect an extension of staff such as would make this possible. I want to suggest to hon. members that the fine words expressed by the minister in introducing this bill will be of little use to the Canadian people unless there is also a sharp increase in the personnel of the department so that the protection of the act as now amended can be better afforded than it has in the past. I make it clear, once again, that in saying this I have no criticism to direct against those who are now working in the department. If there be a criticism here, and I think there is a very strong one, it is of the government, and of parliaments of other years, for not supplying the necessary financial means so that this important task can be carried out.
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the minister on his remarks with regard to the provisions of this bill dealing with the distribution of drug samples, and I trust these provisions will really be carried out. Any druggist in this field, and I must say I have spent some years in the business, will realize what
Food and Drugs Act
a tremendous flood he has to cope with every day of the week. These regulations are long overdue. The testimony given before the Kefauver committee by Dr. James Bowes, a Salt Lake City gynaecologist, showed that he had made a calculation, which I think would be substantiated by almost any doctor in Canada, that if the 150,000 doctors in the United States received the drug advertisements which he himself had received, it would take two railroad cars, 110 large mail trucks and 800 postmen to deliver the daily loads of drug circulars to doctors. Then after being delivered it would take 25 trash trucks to take away the material and to burn it on a dump pile, and the blaze would be seen 50 miles away, so large would it be. The same doctor has calculated that the value of drug samples left in offices of doctors by detail men-that is the polite way of naming salesmen from the drug companies-in one year was $576. If you multiply this by the 150,000 doctors there are in the United States, then the drug industry spent $86 million a year on samples to doctors. I would remind hon. members that this $86 million was paid for, not by the drug companies, but by the purchasers of medical prescriptions, because the drug companies add on the cost of the samples to their cost of operation.
Most of these samples were thrown out, but as I have already said they were paid for by the sick in the cost of their prescriptions. Dr. Bowes has calculated the cost of promoting the drugs in the United States at $210 million a year, not counting subsidies to medical conventions, which are very substantial, or the tremendous expenditure on medical journal advertising. This is more than the $194 million spent in the United States on drug research and more than 10 per cent of the $2 billion annual gross sale of prescription drugs. If this tremendous promotion were discontinued, it would reduce the cost of drugs to the patient by at least 10 cents in every dollar, Dr. Bowes calculated. So, Mr. Speaker, if the minister can do something to bring this distribution of free samples into some reasonable semblance of order, he will be doing the people of Canada a tremendous service. I will wait with interest to see how the regulations will be implemented, and I hope they will be implemented more effectively than in the past.
Mr. Speaker, I am also very interested in the remarks of the minister about the special consideration which will be given to new drugs. Our regulations up to now have supposedly given ample protection to the public. Manufacturers have been required to file with the department a submission containing all available information with regard to the drug in question. Information on experimental and clinical trials involving the drug concerned

Food and Drugs Act
must be supplied. In view of the fact that hundreds and thousands of new drugs are being produced every year, the provisions of the new act are really academic and will be of little value if the department does not have the staff necessary to check into the new drugs which are introduced. Because they have not had the staff up to now, and in fact have had to depend on the honesty, the good will and the objectivity of the people now concerned in the business

the drug companies, who as I have already mentioned are not in the business primarily to look after the patient, but to make a profit.
Although this is not the time to discuss the question of profits, nevertheless they have been very substantial, to say the least. Senator Kefauver estimated that the profits of the United States, and Canadian drug companies are distinguished by one thing only, and that is that they charge 15 per cent more than do the United States drug companies. The United States drug companies' profits have run at about two and a half times what United States business as a whole has been making, whether you calculate them on sales volume, or whether you calculate them on the amount of money invested by the companies in their businesses. So I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that the department will be able really to have a look at the new drugs which are being produced.
The minister has said that our Food and Drugs Act is a model which has been used by countries all over the world. This may be so, but I suggest that the terms of a bill, which may be a model in writing, will mean very little to the people unless they are really observed. For that we need real enforcement of the act, and that will only come when the department has the facilities to do the job- the staff, the research facilities, the laboratories, and everything else which is required. I say again that we have no questions about the technical competence of the department, but we will certainly be asking questions when we come to the estimates with regard to the adequacy of the size of the staff.
I want to say a few words about the reference made in the bill to the drug thalidomide. I do not think I need reargue the matter; it has already been mentioned by almost every speaker. I do not think that we in Canada can be faulted for having permitted use of the drug. From what I have read it seems to me that it was thought, with a good deal of justification, that there had been ample testing of the drug. But as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) has already mentioned, I think we have the right to ask why it took four months, before it was finally withdrawn when pretty
[Mr. Orlikow.l
solid evidence was coming from Europe that there was a good deal of question about the drug. It may be that we did not have the necessary power under the act. It may be that this is the reason that we are now amending the act. We must have had some power, because the drug was finally ordered to be withdrawn, and if we did have the power so to order, why did it take four months to withdraw it? Was it because the department really did not have the legal authority, and they had to go cap in hand and ask or plead with the company concerned, and depend on their good will with the company?
If that is so, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the department should have asked for authority much sooner than it did, and should have demanded from the company concerned that it co-operate much sooner than it did. This question is of tremendous importance to the people, because more and more people are depending for maintenance of their health on these new drugs which are being developed for use. Yet the people have little to say about these drugs. The drugs are prescribed by the doctor for the patient. The patient has no say in what drugs are used. He has no knowledge of them. He has no say in the type of drug which is used. He has no say about whether the drugs prescribed by the doctor will be prescribed under the generic name or the trade name. Yet this is a matter of tremendous importance not only with regard to the health of the patient but with regard to the price; and the price has a good deal to do with the health of the patient. We have had many cases in which patients have been obliged to pay as much as $1, $2 or $3 a day for the use of some of the new drugs such as cortisone or the new antibiotics. Yet in many cases had the doctor prescribed the drug by the generic name the patient could have had the drug at a fraction of the price he was charged. I know of one case which took place while I was still in the business and in which a patient was charged in the neighbourhood of 20 cents a tablet and was using 10 a day. The drug was developed completely in France and was being sold retail in France at that time for 2 cents a tablet. Why did it cost that much here? The reason was that one company had a patent. One company had a complete monopoly to use that product.
In closing I wish to say that I regret the fact that the minister in introducing this bill did not take the opportunity to bring in one which would be broad enough to give the people of Canada the protection they need and to which they are entitled. I refer to protection not only with regard to two or three specific drugs but protection over the

whole field of quality. I think almost as important as protection in terms of quality is protection in the field of price. This is a field in which we in Canada have not even begun to study the tremendous problems which arise and to take advantage of the tremendous and widespread investigations which have been made in other countries.
While I think this bill is a step in the right direction, it is only a very floundering step and is another indication of how the government has failed to take care of a big problem and has dealt with only the beginning of the problem.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank all those who have participated in the debate. I would thank them for the objective way in which they have approached the bill, the amendment now before the house to the Food and Drugs Act. I would point out that when we get into committee I shall be very happy indeed to answer all questions asked in order to give as full a picture as possible concerning the food and drugs branch.
I can assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) that at the time it will be shown that many of the fears he has are groundless. There are one or two things I should like to mention at this stage in closing the debate on second reading. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) expressed an interest in the results of the federal-provincial conference held last August on the subject of assistance to victims of thalidomide malformations, and also enquired about subsequent negotiations which have taken place with respect to this matter.
Food and Drugs Act
I have already made several public statements concerning the conference but I will be happy to summarize developments for the information of the house.
Hon. members may recall that on August 1,
I announced that a conference was being convened with the provinces in order to discuss the most effective methods of providing some measure of relief to those affected by the thalidomide situation. I indicated at that time that the federal government was prepared to share with the provincial governments the cost of providing programs of assistance in this field.
On August 17, a meeting was held in Ottawa at which all of the provinces were represented. In opening the discussions, I outlined the various areas in which the federal government was prepared to make assistance immediately available. These included assessment of individual cases involving medical, psycho-social, and economic features. Transportation costs for infants and parents were also cited as coming within the scope of the federal offer.
I pointed out that various features of the national health grants could be used on a matching basis for surgery, medical care, prosthetic devices, rehabilitation therapy and training. I stated that we would be prepared to ensure that the health grants program was capable of providing this type of assistance and would undertake to make any modifications that might be required. Necessary hospitalization would, of course, be available under the existing federal-provincial insurance agreements.
In addition, the federal government indicated that it was prepared to make funds available on a matching basis through the new welfare grants program with respect to maintenance costs and related welfare services considered essential to the well-being of the malformed children in question. This would include assistance with the cost of care in the child's own home, assistance with maintenance where it is considered to be in the best interests of the child that he or she be placed in a foster home or institution, and assistance with case work and counselling services. It was pointed out that such assistance would not in any sense establish a precedent affecting other welfare programs.
These are the general outlines of the federal offer which I might say was favourably received by provincial representatives and which the latter agreed to present to their governments for immediate consideration.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. B. S. Mackasey (Verdun) for Mr. Lessard (Si. Henry), moved:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately remove all tolls on the Champlain bridge in Montreal and henceforth adopt a uniform policy with respect to tolls on bridges crossing navigable waters so as to avoid, in any particular area, one section of the population being unfairly and arbitrarily dealt with, as is the case for the people being served by the Champlain bridge.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. members of the house for their consideration and tolerance in this particular matter. I for one would have been very upset had this particular notice of motion disappeared from the order paper. Its purpose is to remove the tolls from the Champlain bridge which, as most hon. members know, is the new bridge joining the metropolitan area of Montreal to the south shore. It was opened on June 24, this year. As most hon. members also know, the metropolitan area of Montreal has a population of over 2 million. This population lives on the island of Montreal and therefore it is very obvious what a tremendous role bridges play in the economic growth of that community.
Not only do the bridges leading to it carry thousands upon thousands of workers daily to and from the island, but they are the medium by which thousands of tons of raw materials and finished products are brought to and from great factories. It is no secret that the building of bridges has not kept pace with the economic growth of Canada. For that matter

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
this is true with regard to countries all over the world because the building of new bridges is admittedly a very costly task.
I should like to confine my remarks to three bridges, namely the Victoria bridge, the Jacques Cartier bridge and the Champlain bridge, because these are the three which serve the industrial centre of the island of Montreal. The first of these, the Victoria bridge, was built around the turn of the century primarily as a railway bridge and no amount of modification in subsequent years has done anything to change it from its purpose as a railway bridge to a bridge the prime purpose of which would be the transportation of automobiles.
The Jacques Cartier bridge, built in 1934, is more suitable for motor traffic, but as early as 1950 it became obvious that the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges could not cope with the many thousands of new automobiles being introduced on to the roads. Giant traffic jams were the rule rather than the exception on these bridges. In fact radio commentators spoke with wonder when traffic on the Jacques Cartier bridge was not held up.
Then in 1954 the St. Lawrence seaway became a reality, and I may be excused for saying that I think it is a monument in the history of Canada to a time when we had a government of action rather than a government of words. It quickly became apparent that the St. Lawrence seaway would do much to encourage and foster the potential growth of the south shore and therefore, in conjunction with the building of the St. Lawrence seaway, the Liberal government passed legislation in 1956 providing for the construction of a new bridge. In saying that I would like at the same time to pay tribute to the Conservatives in that when they took office they carried on this legislation. Even if the new Champlain bridge was not opened until a week after the election I congratulate the Conservatives on making a good try and just missing the mark by a few days.
This bridge was primarily designed to alleviate traffic jams on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges, and is ideally located for that purpose. It is situated just a mile or so from the Victoria bridge. It is a magnificent structure and a real tribute to engineering skill in Canada. It is a six-lane bridge which spans the south shore and comes into the heart of Verdun and over into the city of Montreal. As I say, it was ideally designed for the purpose it was to serve. But what is the situation today, six months after it was opened, and why are cars still lined up bumper to bumper on the two old bridges?
It is a standing joke in the city of Montreal that a motorist who drove up from California, upon being asked if he ever felt alone on the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
journey, replied that the only time he felt alone was crossing the Champlain bridge, that in fact for a moment he thought there was a hole in it because there were no cars going with him and no cars approaching him.
I cross the bridge on Sunday mornings and I do not find six, eight, ten or twelve toll booths open. There are usually only one or two.
In its edition of June 2 the Montreal Star had this to say:
-the bridge was built to relieve Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges and to help south shore development. None of these objectives has been achieved. The old bridges are carrying more traffic than ever and south shore development shows few signs of materialization.
Why is this bridge not being used to its full capacity? Certainly we do not need another royal commission on bridges to find out. The answer encompasses two fields, first the tolls and second, the unfinished approaches.
Unfortunately in its haste to build the bridge in time for the last federal election the government forgot the necessity of building adequate approaches; and so, while the population of Montreal can see the bridge from the vantage point of Mount Royal, they have not as yet found out how to get to it. It is a common thing for people to leave their homes on Sunday afternoon and see if they can find the opening to the bridge inside two hours. They exchange views and jokes about it the following Monday, but it is really not a joking matter.
Why are the approaches not ready? The answer is that that spirit of domination which characterized the Prime Minister's behaviour at the commonwealth conference, that same spirit of domination which characterizes the government's negotiations with British Columbia, has permeated to the municipal level and civic authorities are unable to get along with representatives of the harbour board.
One day we find representatives of the city of Montreal telling us in all good faith that a second approach to the bridge is not needed, while the next day representatives of the harbour board say not only are approaches needed but they are actually under construction.
The notice of motion deals specifically with the question of tolls. It is well known that for many years tolls were charged on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. The federal government made repeated requests to Mr. Duplessis, the late premier of Quebec, to co-operate in removing these tolls but always to no avail. Just before the election, however, when surveys showed the
Proposed Abolition of Tolls on Bridges amazing Liberal sweep that became reality in June on the island of Montreal, our Tory friends looked desperately for something to restore their prestige and something to save the seat of the Associate Minister of National Defence. Therefore they approached Mr. Jean Lesage, premier of Quebec with a view to removing the tolls, and to their amazement Mr. Lesage put politics aside. He also realized there was a federal election in the offing and he consented to the alleviation of the tolls on the two older bridges. Here is what the Montreal Star had to say at the time:
There is general happiness, of course, that traffic moves without tolls. But this is tempered, at least among some of those who launched the campaign, by the politics which brought about the desired results... The fact that the southern end of the bridges is in Mr. Sevigny's riding helped too- particularly in view of the date of the federal election, in which the associate minister of defence would like to be returned to parliament. And if any politician has any influence on a political decision relating to his riding it should be a cabinet minister.
Politics is glorious.
So are toll free bridges.
Mr. Speaker, if that was the purpose in removing the tools, at least the government was successful because the associate minister is again a member of this house. But I am more concerned with the injustice that has sprung up as a result of this toll removal. No longer is the new Champlain bridge operating under precisely the same conditions as the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. We have the intolerable effect that the Champlain bridge is now at the disposal of those people who can pay for it, and the ordinary motorist who can ill afford the toll on the Champlain bridge must once again add to the confusion, chaos and over burdening of the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges.
I say that this is an insult, not only to the riding that I represent at the mouth of this particular bridge but indeed to all the taxpayers in the west end of Montreal. Here is a bridge conceived for one particular purpose, to alleviate traffic on the other two bridges. That was its prime objective. Second, it was to encourage development on the south shore. What did the federal government do after rushing the completion of this bridge? They immediately placed it under a handicap so that those people who, for geographical reasons if nothing else, are prone to use this new highway are forced once again to go back to the old structures if they want to avoid this toll which, after all, in this day and age is simply another form of indirect taxation.
There is another effect upon which I would like to dwell, if only for a moment. In their
