Proposed Abolition of Tolls on Bridges
desire for their pound of flesh the government has refused to remove the toll on the bridge so that one can get from one part of the city of Verdun to another. We have a large area called Nuns island that we, the citizens of the mainland of the city of Verdun, must pay a toll on this new bridge to reach. Hence this whole area, crying for development and which could provide thousands of jobs in the housing industry, lies dormant until the government decides to live up to its promise and at least remove the toll on that part of the bridge between Verdun and Nuns island.
I would urge the government to at least rectify their error. There is a growing suspicion in the city, indeed in the whole country I think, that this toll placed on the Champlain bridge is but another manifestation of the inefficiency that has characterized five years of Tory government. I would ask this government to at least show they are big enough to rectify a mistake that no doubt was caused in their haste, in their anxiety to get that big voice of French Canada back into parliament, the Associate Minister of National Defence. Therefore I would urge the government to do three things. First, remove the tolls. Second, speed up the building of the approaches to the bridge; accelerate this by putting more money at the disposal of the city of Montreal and the national harbours board. Third, at least spend a few dollars in an organized campaign for placing advertisements in the local newspapers, the weekly newspapers and spots on the radio, anything that would acquaint the people of Montreal as to just where this beautiful, mysterious bridge is located.
I would suggest to the Minister of Transport for whom I have great respect, that he come down there himself and see just what his record would be in the obstacles race. I assure him that at the present time strangers at the Mount Royal hotel trying to find the Champlain bridge can complete this obstacle course in a little under two hours. I would suggest that the minister come down himself and see if he can better that time. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I think there has been great discrimination against the people of the western part of the island of Montreal for whom this bridge was designed. This toll, besides being a form of indirect taxation, is having the effect of defeating the very purpose for which the bridge was constructed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a point of order at this time. It refers to this resolution and the fact that a private member seeks to change or alter in some way the revenues of the crown. I have not had an opportunity to put


my hand on all the rules in Beauchesne's work with respect to this matter, but I would refer Your Honour to page 214, citation 249 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. Section 2 is pertinent:
A motion requesting the government to introduce immediately legislation granting retirement allowances to all citizens over 60 years of age is out of order because it involves an expenditure of money.
And section 3 of citation 249 is also pertinent in that it declares:
An amendment declaring that government action in any matter should be taken forthwith and giving a direct order which, if approved by the house, would compel the government to adopt measures involving an expenditure of public money, could not be moved by a private member.
On the following page, 215, there is this quotation. I will skip the first part of section 1 of citation 250 and quote this paragraph which is in quotation marks:
"If any motion, or bill, or proceeding is offered to be moved, whether in the house or in a committee, which requires, but fails to receive, the recommendation of the crown, it is the duty of the Chair to announce that no question can be proposed upon the motion, or to direct the withdrawal of the bill. In like manner, after the question has been proposed on an amendment, and it has appeared that the amendment would vary the incidence of taxation or increase the charge upon the consolidated fund, the Speaker has declined to put the question".
Also, Mr. Speaker, in another citation of Beauchesne I recall, although I do not have the exact citation here, that if any amendment or change were to be made similar to this, it would of course have to be made by a minister of the crown. I merely submit, Mr. Speaker, that if this type of resolution was allowed to go forward unchallenged, it might give some precedence for a further motion in this regard. There are probably other hon. members who wish to speak on this resolution, and Your Honour will decide whether you wish to take it under advisement or rule on it at the moment. However, I put this point forward after glancing quickly, as I did, at this resolution.

Proposed Abolition of Tolls on Bridges hon. member, without arguing with him, that if he is in the position of coming into the house, and is first seized with the matter, he could either raise a point of order with regard to it at the first opportunity, by interrupting, the speaker who had the floor, or he could wait until the hon. member who had the floor had finished his speech. As to the other point which the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond put to the Chair, hon. members all recognize the intent of the motion; but in this house, unfortunately, the words of a motion must speak for themselves.
However, I am not going to rule the motion out of order. I will take it under advisement. I find that perhaps the use of the words "should immediately" is not as specific as the-words "the government shall". This may be indulging in semantics. However, I should be prepared, without considering this as a precedent, to let the debate continue. My own view is that the motion could have been better worded, but without considering this as a precedent establishing that an hon. member may move a motion which would affect ways and means, I think the sense of the house is that we deem the motion to be generally in order. Mr. Speaker, the whole problem of bridges and tolls on the island of Montreal should be discussed briefly under two headings. I fully realize the fact that there exists in the country at the present time a paradoxical situation in relation to bridges and public works of this type. On some bridges we have tolls and on others we have none. However, I feel that the problem in relation to Montreal must be discussed with two things in view. First of all, Montreal is an island with a population of over 2 million. In order to get off the island the people must use bridges. There is absolutely no choice involved.
As hon. members who have spoken have already pointed out, we have three bridges in the general area being discussed under the present resolution. Years and years ago the Victoria bridge was constructed. It became extremely antiquated and only recently have conditions been improved on this bridge. After the Victoria bridge, the Jacques Cartier bridge was constructed. Then recently the Champlain bridge was constructed. The situation which exists now, and hon. members have already discussed it, is that tolls have been removed from the Victoria bridge and the Jacques Cartier bridge. What do we see? I agree with the hon. member for Verdun. I travelled on the Champlain bridge the other day. It is extremely difficult to get on to it. I again suggest to him that he use his good offices to correct this situation or to help to correct it. Apart from this fact, however, the fact is that while tolls have been lifted from the Jacques Cartier bridge and the Victoria bridge, traffic is naturally very heavy on them and hardly anybody is using, comparatively speaking, the Champlain bridge. At least up until the present time that is the situation; I do not know whether future conditions will correct it. The government might say that in order to pay for the

construction of the bridge in the future, or in order to amortize the cost, tolls must be maintained. However, I simply suggest that if nobody is going to use the bridge because of the existing situation, we would perhaps only be kidding ourselves by continuing this present comedy. I should therefore like to join with other members in suggesting the abolition of tolls on the Champlain bridge.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before five o'clock I had been outlining, in closing second reading of this debate, the progress and developments at the federal-provincial conference which was held on August 17 in connection with this subject, and I will go on from that point.
Another important subject which came up for discussion at the conference was the problem of obtaining accurate information as to the number of children with malformations associated with the use of thalidomide. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec did not have reliable information on this matter at the time but indicated they were conducting surveys to determine the extent of the situation within their respective jurisdictions. The remaining provinces reported
Food and Drugs Act
that they had information indicating a maximum number of some 15 children where the drug thalidomide had definitely been associated. These appeared to be restricted to western Canada since no cases had been reported from the Atlantic area. I might say that we are still awaiting final word on the number of cases involved on a national basis.
In this connection provincial representatives were informed of the progress being made with respect to a special pilot project which the department had initiated in the Ottawa area some months previously. Carried out with the full co-operation of the local medical profession, pharmacists and hospitals, this study is designed to obtain as much information as possible respecting the distribution of thalidomide and particularly as it might have been used during pregnancy. The project is still under way.
During the meeting several significant steps were suggested and received general acceptance. These had to do with the setting up of national expert committees to foster improvement of knowledge and facilities for dealing with severe disabilities, particularly in young children. Among other things it was proposed that birth records should reflect malformations in greater detail to permit better information being available.
Within a matter of weeks after the August 17 conference all provinces advised us of their willingness to co-operate in this program. As far as the federal government is concerned, of course, we have been ready at any time to act on projects to be submitted by the provinces in respect of individual cases.
Following on the recommendations of the federal-provincial conference, a meeting was convened in Ottawa on September 17 of specialists in the field of rehabilitation. Under the chairmanship of Dr. J. C. Rathbun of London this committee gave careful consideration to the problem of phocomelia rehabilitation and made plans with a view to ensuring the availability at a national level of expert advice on rehabilitation measures and prosthetic devices for children at an early age.
A special subcommittee was established which early in October visited selected centres in the United States in order to obtain the latest information on surgical and rehabilitation procedures and prosthetic appliances. The full committee held a further preparatory meeting in Montreal on November 7 and a third meeting is to be held in Toronto later this month to which provincial representatives have been invited.

Food and Drugs Act
A second expert committee has been established on the subject of congenital anomalies. This will hold its first meeting in Ottawa about the middle of November and will be charged with consideration of all aspects of the occurrence of congenital malformations, and not only those that may be attributal to thalidomide.
I hope that this summary review of steps taken in connection with assistance to thalidomide victims will indicate to the house the vigorous way in which the federal government has exercised leadership in this matter. I am aware, of course, that the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) feels that the federal government should assume "full, final and ultimate responsibility to see that the program of rehabilitation will be carried out". I trust that I have given sufficient evidence to indicate that we have taken a firm lead in this matter and have worked out arrangements co-operatively with provincial authorities with a view to ensuring an effective program.
In placing this undertaking on a joint basis we are following the traditional pattern of health and welfare programs in Canada which I am sure all hon. members will agree have been most successful and effective. The hon. member for York Centre indicated concern about the possibility of difficulty where a parent of a thalidomide victim moved to a province where there had been no necessity for the development of an assistance program. I can only say that we are not unmindful of this type of complication and it is one that is being borne in mind in developing our arrangements with the provinces.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), to whom I extend warm congratulations on his maiden speech in the house, indicated his intention to introduce amendments to cover what he described as "omissions". The government will certainly be very pleased indeed to consider these amendments when they are put forward. In particular he referred to the problem of rapid withdrawal of a drug from the market. As I have mentioned, we are at present awaiting the report of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons on our new drug procedures and this may well be one of the matters that will be dealt with in its recommendations. In any case I can assure the hon. member that the point he has raised will not be overlooked and that in the development of new regulations everything possible will be done to facilitate and expedite whatever action may be warranted. Indeed, the bill in its present form contains authority for prohibition of the sale of a drug under schedule H and this by itself should 
meet the problem in that it makes the sale of such a drug illegal.
The hon. member also suggested that the department should consider placing a special liaison officer in each drug company undertaking the development and evaluation of a new drug. This appears to be a suggestion of some substance. However, I would point out that the clinical testing of new drugs does not take place at the headquarters of the company. While in most cases the bulk of the testing occurs abroad, such testing as is done in Canada of a clinical nature takes place in our larger medical centres. With this in mind I might say that we have been exploring the possibility of establishing closer liaison with these medical centres. I do not wish to elaborate on this matter further at the moment as it may well form one of the principal subjects in the report of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons.
In closing this debate, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my personal appreciation to all hon. members who have supported this measure. I should also like to thank hon. members who have expressed sympathy and understanding with regard to the problem that developed, and particularly those who have urged that the tragedy involved transcends political considerations. Finally, I would express a personal word of congratulation to Dr. Frances Kelsey. Like other hon. members, I am also proud that she is Canadian born. Having regard to the size of the United States, her action may very well have averted what might have been a major catastrophe. I can only commend her for her foresight.

I would suggest to the minister that a committee could be set up under the food and drugs directorate, called the national advisory committee on drugs and prescriptions, consisting of doctors, pharmacists, drug manufacturers, chemists, biologists and, in fact, anybody connected with drugs, their manufacture, use and distribution.
This also deals with samples. At the present time samples are sent out to doctors on a mailing list only after they have already been approved by the food and drugs directorate. Therefore this amendment that is proposed will control only the number of samples which are sent out, but it will not control what samples are sent.

They are also very useful in starting a patient on medication at any time of the night or day when a drug store is not available. They familiarize a doctor with the characteristics of a drug, what it looks like and feels like, and they also at times provide free medication for those patients who cannot afford to have a prescription filled.

Amongst other things, the document points out that the food and drug directorate wrote a letter to the manufacturers to assist them in recalling the drug. The letter included this quotation:

Food and Drugs Act
